---
title: "Screams vs. Laughs"
subtitle: "How American audiences respond to horror and comedy movies"
author: "Zheyre Tolliver"
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
movies <- read_rds("movies.rds")
```

Horror and comedy are two genres built to make us *feel* something: fear in one, laughter in the other. For my final project, I am studying the psychological pull of these genres. To start, I looked at how audiences actually respond to them, using ratings from `r format(nrow(movies), big.mark = ",")` movies on IMDb.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
movies |>
  ggplot(aes(x = votes, y = rating, color = genre)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Comedy = "#e8a33d", Horror = "#7b2cbf")) +
  labs(
    title = "Audiences Rate Comedies Higher Than Horror Films",
    subtitle = "Each dot is one movie released since 1970 with at least 1,000 IMDb votes",
    x = "Number of IMDb votes (log scale)",
    y = "Average IMDb rating",
    color = NULL,
    caption = "Source: IMDb Non-Commercial Datasets"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "top")
```

Each point is one film. Movies further to the right drew more viewers, and movies higher up were rated more favorably.
